Mr. Speaker, I should like to take only a few minutes to indicate my support of Bill C-8, as introduced once again this year by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie). In his various speeches on this bill he has made it clear that it is important for us to be aware of our history and to keep its memory alive. I think that the suggestion he has made is one that should be implemented. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Thunder Bay (Mr. Penner) say that he agreed with the principle of this bill. I was sorry, however, to hear him suggest that we should confine ourselves to an annual one hour in Parliament talking about Sir John A. Macdonald. We all smiled at some of the arguments he put up as to why we should not have a holiday. May I suggest to him that thanks to the foresight of Sir John A. Macdonald, he was bom in the early part of January, so we could arrange, certainly in the parts of the country from which the hon. member for Thunder Bay and I come, for a blizzard to take place

November 24, 1970

on that weekend so that the day will be one on which people stay home and think about our history and not run the risk of the dire catastrophes referred to by the speaker.
You still stay here anyway.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Yes, we can stay here and have a blizzard even in this place. In fact, it might be good for us to have one here once in a while.
I hope that my hon. friend, the hon. member for Hillsborough, will not feel that I am taking some of the time in this hour simply for the purpose of giving the House some useless information, but when he was telling us about the various people who had birthdays on the same day as Sir John A. Macdonald, it led me to pursue still further some research that I was doing in the Canadian Directory of Parliament. This is a book that was published in our centennial year and gives brief biographies of all those who were Members of Parliament during the first 100 years of this nation's history. On going through the book I find that we have had in Parliament since we came into being 45 persons by the name of Macdonald, 29 of them spelled Macdonald and 16 spelled McDonald.
How many were spelled with a capital D and how many with a small d?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
That was the kind of information that I was anxious to complete, but the way this book is set up did not accommodate me on that point. May I point out that in addition to having that number of members by the name of Macdonald we have had eleven John Macdonalds, seven John A. Macdonalds and four John Alexander Macdonalds. So, the place has been overrun. We have two right now as a matter of fact, but we will not go into their biographies at this point.
The hon. member for Thunder Bay had some doubts about having a holiday, but when you look at the total picture, it seems to me it is significant that we should honour our Macdonalds, beginning with the first one.
I wondered about some of the other famous names. I find that we have had only three Lauriers, two Bordens, four Kings, four Bennetts, two St. Laurents and three Pearsons. Thank heaven, as someone will say, we have had only one Diefenbaker and one Trudeau.
How many Knowles?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Four, I believe. If hon. members are interested in this kind of research, I can pass the book around and I am sure that someone else might take away the medal for useless information.
At any rate, even though I have spoken in this light vein, the fact is that not only have we had many Macdonalds in this House of Commons but that the one whose name is mentioned in this bill today has played a significant part in the history of Canada and in the
Public Bills
history of North America, and I believe we should honour his memory in the way suggested in this bill.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Mr. James Hugh Faulkner (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I would like to make a few comments on this bill. I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). That was one of the most interesting speeches and useful contribution of information that he has made in the House in a long time. I am sorry that the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) called for the question when he saw me rise because I was impressed by the argument adduced by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) that in view of the fact we are not dealing with one birthday but a variety of birthdays, and among them are included the birthday of the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell) and the hon. member for St. John's East, it makes the over-all proposition more compelling than it was before.
I might start by paying tribute to the hon. member for Hillsborough. If one looked objectively around the House for a suitable apologist for Sir John A. Macdonald one would be hard pressed to improve upon the happy choice of circumstances which have led to the hon. member for Hillsborough being the apologist that we have.
You mean eulogist.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Eulogist or apologist. Not only has he, to many of us, embodied some of the finer qualities that we associate with Sir John A. Macdonald in his own presence, but also he demonstrates those qualities of moderation to which he referred and qualities of middle of the road moderation, as he described it, plus the jovial, erudite and good natured exterior which makes the total man so attractive. I also admire his persistence, because I do not know if all members of the House are aware of the fact that this is not the first time the hon. member for Hillsborough has introduced a bill to create a Sir John A. Macdonald day and if my instinct is correct it will probably not be the last. He has done it over a period of years, and prior to his efforts there were other members who have done the same.
In an effort to brief myself on the complete significance of the debate in which I intended to participate I reviewed previous debates. It seems to me that one of the problems which has persistently hampered his efforts is that this is a popular measure and there have constantly been more people interested and talking about it than there was available time.
I reviewed the speeches back in 1964. The hon. member attracted some very strong support in favour of his efforts. At that time the hon. member for Renfrew North, the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) spoke on the subject. That is an interesting speech for private members to read because it gives new members an idea of how private members' hour can be used to discuss a variety of subjects, not necessarily the

November 24, 1970
Public Bills
subject immediately before the chamber. In fact, reading the remarks of the then hon. member for Renfew North I was not sure whether he was speaking about Sir John A. Macdonald Day or St. Patrick's Day. In the course of developing his argument he quoted a wide variety of historical sources from Pliny the Younger to Henry Ford, who described history as bunk.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Not only did we have speeches from the hon. member for Renfrew North, who is the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, but also from a gentleman who is now Premier of Nova Scotia. Reading his remarks it is difficult to know whether he was more enamoured by the concept of Sir John A. Macdonald or Joseph Howe. It was an interesting debate in so far as it revealed a great deal about private members' hour.
The idea of a national day for Sir John A. Macdonald creates a number of interesting questions, Mr. Speaker, but I do not intend to deal with them all. Aside from the merits of the man himself and his particular and unique position in Canadian history, one of the really compelling arguments is the broader idea of recognizing in a suitable way those Canadians who have made a remarkable and unique contribution to our history.
As a part-time teacher, one of the things that I find depressing about our situation in Canada is not so much the absence of heroes but that we do not seem to know very much about any Canadians who have made a contribution. This is probably as much the fault of our publishing industry, boards of education, departments of education or to the shortage of interested and creative authors, as anything. The fact remains, however, that Canadians generally are not too conscious of figures of historical importance. What is worse, they are not aware of the rather unique qualities of the Canadian historical process, not just the evolutionary constitutional process which is dealt with in university courses but some of the very particular qualities of our history. I do not think it is possible to overcome this by agreeing to a Sir John A. Macdonald Day. As we have already noticed, there would be a variety of claims from different members of this House for other heroes who more closely reflect different political affiliations. I am sure J. S. Woodsworth might have some support in the House, as certainly would Sir Wilfrid Laurier and some others.
In discussing the merits of this particular case we expose a real problem within our country that in our schools, universities and the population at large there is an appalling ignorance of our history, of our antecedents and of the process that led to the development of our country. It may not be argument sufficient to justify Sir John A. Macdonald Day, but it is sufficient for everybody to examine what is going on in the country and ensure that something be done not in a chauvinistic way but in a rational and broad minded way to overcome this deficiency. It could instil in Canadians an understanding and appreciation for the history of their country and in particular for the people who made the important decisions at various times in its development.
Mr. Speaker, when I started making a few notes for this debate today, having lost the notes I had prepared for the three previous aborted sessions we had, I sent to the reference library for some material.
What about Information Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: As I understand it, Mr. Speaker, Information Canada is not dealing essentially with Sir John A. Macdonald.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: They will tell you about Laurier and Trudeau.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I was going to add that, but I thought it had better come from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). One of the documents the library sent me is very interesting. It is entitled "The Dominion Campaign! Sir John Macdonald on the questions at issue before the people. The Premier's great speech before the workingmen of Toronto." Inside is the title "A brilliant review of the vital issues of the present Campaign." I am not sure who published it, but I could hazard a guess.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Information Canada!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: What is particularly interesting about this speech is the first two pages. Unlike the speeches today, in that day they used to add the audience response to the remarks made by the speaker.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
We are probably just as lucky that it is not done, today, but in Sir John A's day there was no risk apparently. In the first page he has one "loud laughter", one "loud cheers", one "laughter", one "cheers and laughter", one "renewed laughter" and one "great cheering". On the second page he has one "hear, hear and applause", five "cheers", one "loud cheers" and two "applause".
This occurs throughout the speech, Mr. Speaker, and is characteristic of the quality of the speech. But one thing I ran across is a familiar argument to people in public life. He was explaining his record to the workingmen of Toronto and was caught in the ambivalent position of all politicians in power, that of trying to claim credit for great achievement and explaining away those areas where there was not achievement. He said: Why then, I ask, has not more been done?
Three years Is a short time, but in three years much has been done.
Mr. Speaker, the argument will come as a surprise to you. It was:
Because we have had an unscrupulous opposition: because we have had an unpatriotic opposition.

November 24, 1970

It was as it says, Mr. Speaker, "A brilliant review of the vital issues of the present campaign," but it reminded me very much of political speeches I have heard in more recent times.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: In Peterborough?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Never in Peterborough.
There are two particular points to be considered in dealing with this man. If you read this material about Sir John A. Macdonald and read some of his speeches, one of the facts that impresses itself upon you is the extraordinary relevance of what he said at that time to the situation today, particularly in two areas that have been alluded to. One is that he was a nationalist, and the other is that he understood the rights of the minority as few Canadians have done. He understood the significance of language rights. If we had only had the wisdom as a people to follow the advice of Sir John A. Macdonald on language rights and minority rights, we would have largely eliminated the problems we face in this country today.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I should like to turn briefly to his record as a nationalist and the relevance of that today. One authority on Sir John A. Macdonald, of course, is the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). In the debates of January 11, 1967, commemorating the 152nd anniversary of the birthday of Sir John A. Macdonald, the right hon. member for Prince Albert said:
-his principle for Canada, that it must be an independent nation on the north half of the North American continent willing to co-operate in freedom but insisting on the right that policies for Canada be made by Canadians. That was his contribution.
Mr. Speaker, that has extraordinary relevance to Canada and to Canadians today. He rejected the liberal option of that day of free trade. In many ways that option could be viewed, to use modern language, as the continentalist option today. He rejected it then, and many of us who are looking at a similar proposition in contemporary terms are wondering if we should not be equally vigilant against the continentalist option. For that reason Sir John A. Macdonald's relevance today is undisputed.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I read an article in Maclean's about the formation of a committee for an independent Canada. I suggest that if Sir John A. Macdonald were alive today, he would be a charter member of the committee for an independent Canada. As one reviews the eight-point program of that group it becomes clear that the nationalist position has as much relevance today as the nationalist policy had in 1878 and in subsequent elections. I will not go into the program of the committee for an independent Canada.

Please do.
Public Bills

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Those who are concerned about the classic problem of Canadian national identity and Canadian policy could well review this program in light of some of the advice given by Sir John A. Macdonald.
I should like to make another point which deals with the other element of his policy. This, too, is extremely relevant to our scene today. I am speaking of his policy in the area of language rights. He made a great speech on February 17, 1890, in which he dealt with language rights in the Northwest Territories. The hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) pointed out very ably the circumstances in which he made the speech. Considering the prevailing degree of religious bigotry that characterized not only this country but other countries, the degree of distrust that characterized relations between language groups and religious groups in this country, when Sir John spoke in this area, and particularly when he spoke in a way that had a particular affect on his following within his own party, he acted with extraordinary wisdom and courage. As I said before, if we had only had the wisdom to follow the example of Sir John A. Macdonald on this delicate question throughout our history, many of the problems that plague us today would not exist. In his speech on February 17, 1890, he said:
I have no accord with the desire expressed in some quarters that by any mode whatever there should be an attempt made to oppress the one language or to render it inferior to the other; I believe that would be impossible if it were tried, and it would he foolish and wicked if it were possible. The statement that has been made so often that this is a conquered country is d propos de rien. Whether it was conquered or ceded, we have a constitution now under which all British subjects are in a position of absolute equality, having equal rights of every kind- of language, of religion, of property and of person.
If we had had the wisdom to follow the principle of the first, second and fourth points, our history until 1970 might have been somewhat different and, hopefully, somewhat happier. Throughout the speech-and it is a speech of wisdom and courage-he asks: Why is language so important to individuals? Halfway through the speech he says:
Why, Mr. Speaker, if there is one act of oppression more than another which would come home to a man's breast, it is that he should be deprived of the consolation of hearing and speaking and reading the language that his mother taught him. It is cruel. It is seething the kid in its mother's milk. The greatest, perhaps, of all the objections to this measure is that it is a futile measure. It will not succeed.
He understood precisely the significance of language for our people. Our failure in part to understand this has puzzled me in the debate we have had in recent years on language rights. I happen to be one whose mother tongue is the tongue of the majority in this country, if one likes to put it that way; yet I know the umbrage and strength of feeling I would bring to bear if I were in the minority position and my right to use the language in which I had been raised, which embodies the heritage of which I am proud, were interfered with in any way. My feelings would be as strong as the feelings of the people wo are in the minority position.
Sir John A. Macdonald had the wisdom to see the importance of the question and to see its relevance to our

November 24, 1970
Public Bills
confederation. He had the courage to pursue a principle that was unpopular in its day but is tremendously relevant to our history. That is all I wish to say, Mr. Speaker. I have enjoyed participating in this debate. Since there are others who wish to speak, I shall take my seat. I end by saying that in the areas of nationalism and language rights, Sir John A. Macdonald is as relevant today as he was more than 100 years ago.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must advise the House that the Parliamentary Secretary's time has expired and he would need unanimous consent in order to answer the question. Is that agreed?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary mentioned in a very serious and proper way what Sir John A. Macdonald had done for us with respect to unity and language. Does he not also agree that if we had followed his advice in other respects there would be no Grits or teetotallers in this country today?
I will drink to that.

Mr. Speaker, I think Sir John A. Macdonald would have appreciated thoroughly the flavour of this debate. He would have said, "Oh, well, it is almost six o'clock and this measure has not passed. Perhaps it will pass some other time- hopefully, tomorrow."
I am pleased to second the continuing effort of the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) to pay tribute to Sir John and his attempt to allow all Canadians to pay tribute to the man who put Canada together. I, too, had the pleasure of going to Kingston and taking part in the ceremony performed each year by the Kingston Progressive Conservative Association to do honour to Sir John A. Macdonald. I think even hard-shelled Grits could gain something from making a pilgrimage to that city. They have there a fantastic graveyard, and if we must go to one, and we all shall one day, we might as well go to one as fine as that. The ceremony is sincerely staged by the Conservative Association with the help of cadets wearing uniforms of former times.
Then, of course, there are the speeches-one was made this year by my hon. friend from Hillsborough and one was made last year by myself-that go back a considerable time. I suggest that the Grits could very usefully see our ceremony and hear us pay tribute to Sir John and, in return, we would be glad to attend their ceremony when they pay their annual respects to Sir Wilfrid Laurier. We would be glad to accompany them at that time.
I think one of the most moving experiences I had during the 1967 centennial celebrations was seeing costumed actors of Canada visit Halifax and play the roles of the Fathers of Confederation. The man who played Sir
John A. Macdonald was Robert Christie. It so happens, I think, that Mr. Christie is a teetotaller or as near a teetotaller as one can imagine, if one can imagine such a
state.
I can't imagine it.

The man who played George Brown, another great figure of that time, I will not name. George Brown, as everyone knows, was the founder of the Globe and Mail and, as one can imagine, he had no use for booze whatsoever. The actor who played him had a great deal of use for booze. Therefore, the teetotaller was playing Sir John A. Macdonald and the tippler was playing the part of George Brown. It added a certain merriment to the evening when these "Fathers of Confederation" sat down with the citizens of our day. I recall it because Christie did a very good job of playing the part of Sir John A. Macdonald. That Halifax audience responded in a way in which I have rarely seen an audience respond to an actor. Their attention was riveted on Robert Christie. If he did epitomize Sir John A. Macdonald, one could imagine the magic hold that Sir John A. had on people. I understand that Mr. Christie spent a considerable amount of time learning Sir John A's mannerisms. Therefore, he may be the nearest that any of us will ever see approaching the mannerisms of Sir John A. I was tremendously impressed.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I support the efforts of my hon. friend. Anyone who has visited the office of the hon. member for Hillsborough, one of the original settlers in the West Block, will have noticed a plaque on his wall from one of the early election campaigns. It is a picture of Sir John A. Macdonald leading the successful Conservative party with the words, "The old flag; the old policy; the old leader". In 100 years people have gone from the belief in established things to the point where in the last election the successful party brought someone in from virtually under the rug, one who probably was not known to most Canadians. It is an interesting reflection on how political techniques have changed. In past years people voted for something in which they believed; now they will accept almost anything born in the age of advertising, any charismatic promise. I will not get into a discussion on advertising. I will do that when the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) introduces his bill in that regard.
I vigorously support the bill of the hon. member for Hillsborough. It may be all very well for each party to espouse its own heroes but with this bill we are doing more than just paying tribute to Sir John A. Macdonald, the greatest Conservative of all. We are asking Parliament to recognize the fact that confederation, the union of provinces from the Atlantic to the Pacific, is really his handiwork. Oddly enough, at one stage of his career Sir John A. had no use for the concept of confederation. He then saw it as the means of solving the great instability between the quarrelsome Canadians in Quebec and Ontario. Once he set his foot on the path toward confederation, he used his skills and ability to bring it about.

November 24, 1970

Great persons such as George Brown were associated with him in that endeavour. I am sure that historians in this House, including the hon. member for Hillsborough, will agree that if Sir John A. had no1 set the course for confederation it would not have been accomplished, or would have come about in a vastly different form. Such was his ability to deal with people. Above all, he was a master at dealing with people. Long nights spent sitting around tables with the conversation flowing as freely as the wine may have been responsible; I do not know. Sir John A. was not a great orator. I understand that his speaking technique was to stand, more or less turn his back on the opposition and speak in somewhat confidential voice to his followers, urging them to support some sensible measure which he was introducing.
I hope we will not be waylaid into choosing heroes of the various parties, laudable though that may be. What we are now discussing is paying tribute to the one person who created confederation.

Mr. Speaker, in light of the Conservatives' singular lack of success in recent elections, I suppose it is appropriate that the day which they celebrate each year should take place in a graveyard. I in part support the principle of this bill, but I would have been happier if it had been founded upon the premise of a Prime Minister's Day rather than a Sir John A. Macdonald Day.
I have done some reading and research concerning Sir John A. Macdonald. I feel if this suggestion had been made to him personally, his answer would have been decisive, abrupt, eloquent, clear, rude and it probably would have been "No". I think Sir John A. Macdonald would be more pleased that we have seen fit to name an icebreaker after him, in keeping with the independent and pioneering spirit of this man.
If this bill had suggested a Prime Minister's Day, tribute could have been paid to the former member for Lambton West, the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie. We recognize that a politician who beats another politician deserves some credit and it should not be forgotten that Sir Alexander Mackenzie did, in fact, defeat Sir John A. Macdonald.

speechtext:
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that Bill C-181, to provide tem-
Public Order Act, 1970
porary emergency powers for the preservation of public order in Canada, be read the third time and do pass.
And the amendment thereto of Mr. Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands).

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before five o'clock I was indicating to the House that the bill we are discussing is not, in a sense, a new bill or some strange measure introduced for the first time, but a bill to replace the War Measures Act presently in force. I was dealing with the question of possible abuse raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas). It is true there are bound to be abuses and that some people will be arrested who should not have been arrested. The question we have to decide is what type of abuse there is to be. In the absence of a bill of this type there will be abuses by the FLQ, because this is what Bill C-181 is about: it is not legislation in a vacuum; it deals with a specific problem. I am sure there is a problem in Quebec, and it is one which arises because of the FLQ. The hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) and the other hon. member who spoke from the Conservative side of the House made certain remarks about the merging of separatists with the FLQ. Let me remind hon. members that the aim is still separatism; what we object to are the means by which to bring about separatism.
The amendment seeks the provision of some sort of safeguard, one which would amount, I suggest, to a pretrial trial. Hon. members with legal training on both sides of the House will know that one thing the common law does not tolerate in criminal matters is a trial before a trial. The speeches made before the amendment was moved indicated there should be some body, some committee, which would investigate not only the condition of prisoners, whether they had been given an opportunity to get in touch with their relatives and solicitors, but also to find out whether or not they should have been arrested. But how would the committee, or commission, find this out? By guesswork? Prisoners do not wear labels on their coats.
The only way to find out would be by investigation and getting evidence. However, evidence obtained in this way would not be in the purview of a court. Let us say the committee decided that a person under detention had been properly arrested. What bearing would this have on his subsequent trial? A committee would already have reached the conclusion that he ought to have been arrested and, as I say, it is one of the principles of our law that a person to be tried should be tried in the courts where he has an opportunity to examine witnesses and bring forward evidence. I should like the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands to tell me how this committee or board would do its work without getting into a pre-trial trial which is obnoxious to our system of law.

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext: It is obvious, when you think about it.

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) will have an opportunity to let us know how this is to be done. I have heard these points of view expressed over and over again. There are some, Mr. Speaker, who

November 24, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
think they have a monopoly of conscience, a monopoly of concern for the rights of citizens. They do not. We are all seriously concerned with this aspect of the bill. I am sure the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) struggles with the thought that after 800 years of striving for civil liberty, the rights of citizens are being placed in jeopardy for a short time. But we have to make up our minds. Shall we allow a party or group to use bombs, violence and kidnapping to attain a certain end, an end which would obviously mean the destruction of Canada, or should we use every means at our disposal to prevent this happening?
We on this side have thought this out. We, too, have struggled with our consciences and we have concluded there is only one way to deal with the situation, and that is to make illegal the fraternity or group of people who are dedicated to the overthrow of this nation by threats and by violence. I would not have supported this bill if it concerned merely an attack on property rights or something of that nature. But something else is involved. The obvious purpose, and the only purpose of the FLQ is to achieve an end which is the destruction of Canada as we know it by using ways and means which we consider obnoxious and dangerous.
I urge all members of the House, if they cannot accept this bill, to say so and vote against it. Let them not delay it, though, and allow the War Measures Act to remain in force while they continue to expound the same points. I do not for one minute suggest that anyone in this House or on the other side is trying to delay the passage of this measure for a political purpose; I believe legislation of this nature is too serious for that. Everybody here is wrestling with his conscience in an attempt to decide whether or not to support the bill. Surely, though, an answer must come one way or another and we must take our stand and determine whether or not the FLQ shall be allowed to use the methods it has used in the past, or whether we should say: No, we cannot allow the destruction of this nation by violence, threats, kidnapping and murder.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment currently under study reads as follows:
That Bill C-181 be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House for the purpose of reconsidering clause 12 with a view to the inclusion therein of a provision for the establishment of an independent body to review the administration under the said bill.
Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of this amendment which provides for the establishment of such a body for three reasons. First of all, we are all human beings and for that reason we may all make mistakes, whatever our chosen field of endeavour. Secondly, owing to the nature of their work, policemen are more liable to make mistakes than other people. Their having to work fast makes them all the more liable and the fact that we live in a bilingual country does not make their work any easier.
We all remember the case of the minister from British Columbia who was arrested in Quebec City last spring
and put in jail simply because the officers who arrested him could not speak English. They did not understand him when he explained.
I myself speak only French, and on two occasions in one week I had troubles with the police, because Ottawa police officers, who spoke only English, pressed two charges against me.
Unfortunately, policemen work under a system of quotas, that is, in order to get promotions, they must make a certain number of arrests.

Trusting that you will give this request your attention, I remain, Rene Matte, M.P. for Champlain.

A letter will reach Mr. Godin in the near future from the Magistrate's Court, explaining that the notice of payment was sent to him in error.

November 24, 1970

I regret any inconvenience this may have caused you and rest assured that all necessary steps will be taken to remedy this.

Retroactive legislation is always wrong. Retroactive criminal legislation is particularly obnoxious and unjust. There can be no argument about the retroactivity of clause 8 of the bill. If the minister had accepted the amendment of the hon. member for Broadview it would have been a different story, but he did not. I am speaking about a person who participated or was present at a number of meetings of the unlawful association, spoke publicly in advocacy of the unlawful association and communicated statements at a time when the association was not unlawful. That is the retroactivity feature of this clause.
The precedent that clause 8 would establish is very regrettable. A precedent will be set that if an organization is declared illegal at some date, after it has been declared illegal we can add that anyone who participated in its activities before it was declared illegal is guilty of an offence. That method is used by dictators throughout the world to stifle freedom of speech and intimidate freedom of association and expression of opinion. Dictatorships throughout the world have done that. 8. In any prosecution for an offence under this Act, evidence that any person, either before or after the coming into force of this Act,

Mr. Speaker, I shall limit my comments to the first part of that clause. In my view, retroactive legislation, as evidenced by precedents, is not an usual feature of our legal system of criminal law.
In that respect, clause 8 is a precedent, an exception. The retroactivity of the legislation becomes necessary in special circumstances where the security of the state may be jeopardized. As for criminal law, the retroactivity of a legislation has seldom been invoked.
When I read clause 8, I thought in the first place, owing to the troubles in Quebec and the extremely confused, anarchic and dangerous conditions, that to my regret I would have to accept the retroactivity of the bill since that measure was quite unusual and could be a dangerous weapon in the hands of the government.

Being a Quebecker, what hurts me most is the will of the government to bring the people of Quebec to heel and to keep them within Confederation against their wishes. And now the government wants to use this

retroactive clause to condemn and to hunt down any individual opposed to the established order.

Those who might have objected during the present crisis are definitely the convicted ones and we readily agree to this proposal. Article 11 reads as follows:
1.	Everyone charged with a penal offence has the right to be presumed innocent until proven guilty according to law in public trial at which he has had all the guarantees necessary for his defence.
2.	No one shall be held guilty of any penal offence on account of any act or omission which did not constitute a penal offence, under national or international law at the time when it was committed. Nor shall a heavier penalty be imposed than the one that was applicable at the time the penal offence was committed.

What in fact the amendment seeks to do is remove clause 8 of this bill, which in effect states that what a person did yesterday today becomes a crime. I want to make it quite clear that we are not here referring to activities and acts which in the past have in fact been crimes, when people committed acts of terror whether by way of bombings or harassment of one kind or another, or caused a social disturbance or the more serious crimes, for instance, of kidnapping, threat to kidnap, physical assault or murder. Those offences have been well known to the body politic and have been offences not just for decades but in most cases for centuries.
What is being attempted through this clause we are seeking to amend is, in effect, to establish that membership in a particular organization and evidence of that membership, which may go back a number of years, is sufficient to convict a person of a criminal offence. That, I think, must be regarded not only as a serious step but one which is particularly offensive. I think, too, in this context we must realize that the precedent it establishes is surely one of the most shocking that we could consider. By allowing this legislation to pass we will be, in effect, allowing a precedent to be established that a person who may hold a particular belief or who has participated in a particular organization may find that while it may not be a criminal offence at the present time, two years from now or ten years from now Parliament may be able to say, "We now consider membership in or support of this organization or its ideals to be crime."
I think we only have to look at the fact that there has been almost no definition of what the FLQ stands for to realize how broad and how vague that kind of implication can be. We are asked, in effect, to allow the authorities to arrest men and women on the evidence of having attended a meeting or two of this organization two years ago, five years or seven years ago. We are being asked to agree that someone who may have in an informal conversation with a friend half a dozen years ago spoken well of this organization should be regarded now as having committed a criminal offence.
Because this clause refers to a communicative statement, we are being asked to regard even those who transmitted information relating to this organization as having committed a criminal offence. While the Minister of Justice has argued that it is now clearly stated that a simple transmission of this information, without doing it for propaganda purposes, would not constitute a crime, we only have the minister's words in the House in that regard. But we know only too well that when statutes are being interpreted in the courts, only what is in the statutes counts and no desire expressed in this House will affect that interpretation one way or another.
Perhaps most shocking in regard to this retroactive clause 8 is the fact that the government was unwilling to even provide a time limit. It is known to almost everyone in this country that before the month of October those who belonged to or participated in the organization

November 24, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
known as the FLQ, unless they were then participating in accepted criminal activity were not regarded as having done anything illegal. We know of people who have been close to some of the parties in this government who have over the years participated in the FLQ without in themselves having committed a criminal offence.
Now we are being told that if at any time an individual before the month of October participated in, spoke on behalf of or transmitted information with regard to this organization he is liable to a five year term of imprisonment and a substantial fine. How far back are the authorities going? Since there has been difficulty in apprehending some of the individuals who have been directly involved in recent FLQ activity as frustrations and suspicions have increased, we know how much easier it might be to go back and root out these individuals. It might be much easier to go back further in order to deal with those who perhaps at an earlier time, without any thought of participating in a criminal organization, lent their support however briefly it may have been to this organization. Are they to be convicted because of that earlier act or innocent involvement?
One could even ask the question: How widely will this clause be interpreted? The minister has said from time to time in the House that he is not only talking about the FLQ per se, but about a successor or an allied organization. What does that mean, and what will it mean in the interpretation of this statute? What kind of definition or what kind of limits will be set if evidence is gathered about the activities of people? maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-SUGGESTED RETENTION OF RADAR AND COMMUNICATIONS SCHOOL AT CLINTON
NATIONAL DEFENCE-SUGGESTED RETENTION OF RADAR AND COMMUNICATIONS SCHOOL AT CLINTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I addressed a question to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) in which I asked him to consider keeping the radar and communications school at the Canadian Forces base at Clinton rather than moving it to Kingston. The Canadian Forces base at Clinton is scheduled for phasing out in September of next year. This question is urgent and proper because last Thursday night, the last day on which the House sat and the minister was in the House, it was announced on the news that the Department of National Defence was to begin construction shortly at the Canadian Forces base at Kingston, at a cost of $1,200,000, for accommodating the radar and communications school which is being moved from the Clinton Canadian Forces base which is scheduled for closure in 1971.
There were many other reasons for asking the question. I was told by the former Minister of National Defence, when there were rumours last June, that there would be new construction but there would be only minor renovations made to the Kingston base to house this school. Therefore, I did not feel quite so badly. Many months ago I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamie-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
son) to place a new air services training school for the training of air traffic controllers at Clinton in order to keep something operating at the base. This came up previously when consideration was given to spending $6 million on a new building to do this.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I was turned down at that time, but in the meantime Treasury Board refused to grant the Department of Transport the $6 million and told them they should use existing facilities. I immediately wrote the Minister of Transport and requested that another look be given to the Canadian Forces base at Clinton. I received an answer to my letter from the Department of Transport, dated June 19, which stated:
Reference is made to your letter of April 30, 1970, concerning the possibility of the facilities at Canadian Forces base, Clinton, being suitable for the proposed air services training school.
Treasury Board has requested that the feasibility of joint civilian-military air traffic control training be investigated. The decision in this matter could have a major impact on the type of training facility required. Accordingly, consideration of your proposal regarding the use of the Clinton base will be deferred.
The minister goes on to say that he expects a decision to be made about the middle of the summer. I waited until the middle of the summer, and the feasibility study was carried out by the department. I can report on some of the recommendations that were made. The first was that military-civil air traffic control training be combined, and that a common manual of operations for Canadian air traffic control be developed: standard military deviations from the norm shall be noted therein. The recommendations went on to say that an investigation into surplus buildings and suitable sites for an air traffic control school should be completed by December 15, 1970, which is yet to come.
Naturally, the Department of National Defence is involved in any suggestion that would combine the training of military and civilian air traffic control. I am advised by the minister that that study is now being carried out by his department. I am sure that the completion of this study, in co-operation with the Department of Transport, will affect the decision as to where the training will be carried out.
The fact that the station in Clinton was built for radar and communications would make it most suitable for carrying out training. Many of the facilities and training requirements are similar to those used for training at the radar and communications school. It would be sensible and reasonable to have both carried out at that site if the decision is that civil and military air traffic control training should be combined and carried out at the existing location.
Furthermore, we have investigated further requirements for the base after it is closed, or even before, and that is at Conistoga College which is a community college which serves the Huron County area. They have already put in their requirements, at my request, as to how much of the base they might be able to use if it is not to be used fully in the way I have suggested. This matter is

I am not in any hurry for an answer so long as it is the right one, but the people in the area are becoming quite concerned and they hope to have an answer as soon as possible. I suggest that an answer should be given early in the new year. I am trying to establish that this question is urgent. In my opinion it should have been allowed by the Speaker. In any case, this adjournment debate gives me a little more time to deal with the matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-SUGGESTED RETENTION OF RADAR AND COMMUNICATIONS SCHOOL AT CLINTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Forces base, Clinton, is mainly devoted to giving training in radar and communications. For a considerable period of time the Canadian forces activities for training in that field have been divided between Clinton and Kingston.
It had also been evident for some period of time that it would be desirable to consolidate the technical training, and the fact that the military reason and requirement for training provided at Clinton would no longer be required in the near future made it possible to consolidate the operation at Kingston for reasons of economy.
The hon. member referred to the fact that there would be a capital expenditure at Kingston of $1,298 million for the purpose of establishing the consolidated facilities in that city. I would point out that as a result of the closure of Clinton there will be a net saving in annual costs of $2.9 million. In other words, the annual saving from closing the base will be more than twice the amount expended in the first year in putting into effect the training facilities. I might point out to the hon. member, if he does not already know, that the department has been active in locating civilian personnel in other employment.
With regard to his request for the school for air traffic controllers, I should point out that he has a competitor in the field, because the provincial government of Prince Edward Island has made clear its feeling that the air traffic controllers' school should be located at Summer-side and this has been supported by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald). We will be in touch with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) on this question and will give favourable consideration to both possibilities when the time comes to decide the location of the aircraft controllers' facility.

maintopic: AIR TRANSPORT-INSTALLATION OF RADIOS AND HOMER BEACON DEVICES ON PRIVATE COMMERCIAL PLANES
AIR TRANSPORT-INSTALLATION OF RADIOS AND HOMER BEACON DEVICES ON PRIVATE COMMERCIAL PLANES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks tonight concern homer devices to be installed on private commercial planes. I am no expert on the subject, but my interest was prompted by my concern for a lost helicopter pilot whose wife happened to be from my riding. It might interest hon. members of the Conservative party to know that he was formerly the pilot of the

right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). This man was lost in the bush area of northern Saskatchewan for 21 days before the search was called off by the search and rescue section of the Department of National defence.
The area covered by the search seemed to me to be extensive, although it was considered by Search and Rescue as limited. Seventy-two thousand square miles were covered twice by search and rescue planes, but during the 21 days there was no sign of the lost pilot and the search was called off. Finally the miracle occurred and the pilot, because he was wise in the ways of the bush, walked out of the bush 30 pounds lighter. Everybody was pleased to learn that he was still alive.
After discussions with a number of people it seems to me that there is in this regard a tremendous expense to the Department of National Defence and also a tremendous risk to the pilots of Search and Rescue. It also seems to me that in this day of sophisticated, technical knowledge we might expect some of this technology to be used to assist pilots lost in a country as vast as ours.
My investigations reveal that the pilot had flown from his base during a white-out and was without radio or homing device of any kind. Upon further investigation I was appalled to learn that the Department of Transport regulations do not prescribe even such fundamental lifesaving devices as radio or, indeed, any kind of homing device. Why not? Lost planes are common, especially in British Columbia and Ontario. Why are regulations not necessary, not only to save the lives of people who are lost but also to protect people who by nature of their occupation have a professional duty to find them? On November 6, I put a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) and part of this answer was as follows:
The difficulty is that at the moment there is no such assurance of proper standards and we would not want, for example, to require their installation and perhaps give people a false sense of security which, indeed, the equipment now available might not be able to provide.
That seems reasonable enough. We are aware, of course, that all military and commercial transport aircraft using IFR-those letters stand for "Instrument Flight Rules"-are equipped with CPI, otherwise known as Crash Protection Indicator devices. Unfortunately, these devices cost approximately $10,000 each to instal. This amount, of course, is far beyond the reach of many private and small commercial aircraft operators, the loss of whose aircraft causes so much anguish and difficulty to the Department of National Defence. That, I think, is reasonable to assume.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I think we all should examine the criteria necessary for VFR, or aircraft using visual flight rules, the losses among which are probably far greater than among aircraft, the pilots of which can fly on instruments. I have a letter from a constituent of mine which reads in part:
When our own and other companies' personnel got together, discussions often centered around two points; firstly the difficulty associated with suitable crash detection gear, i.e., Sarah & Dart. It was generally agreed that before such a device could be made compulsory by the DOT it would have to meet the following standards-
November 24, 1970

The device must be light and small enough so as not to rob valuable pay-load space. It must be sufficiently inexpensive for private and commercial operators. It must produce a signal, audible or visual, which can be picked up by other VFR aircraft. And, above all, it must be 100 per cent efficient.
In the time remaining I think I ought to elaborate a little on these points. My constituent, incidentally, has submitted an experimental device and I think the Department of Transport would be well advised to assist in the development and research of devices of this kind which do not seem to be available at present. All Canadian flyers and all those interested in aviation ought to be concerned about this matter. I think many other groups are concerned. In conclusion I wish to quote from a booklet entitled "British Columbia Chamber of Commerce, General Policy Statements and Resolutions, 197071". On page 11 the following notation appears: RECOMMENDED
That the government of Canada require all aircraft operating in Canada to be equipped with crash position indicator or homing beacon device.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerard Duquei (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: AIR TRANSPORT-INSTALLATION OF RADIOS AND HOMER BEACON DEVICES ON PRIVATE COMMERCIAL PLANES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the specific subject matter, that of issuing regulations requiring all aircraft using Canadian airways to instal homer beacon devices, has been raised several times in the House. It is an important matter and it is one which the Department of Transport has been directly concerned with for a number of years. I congratulate the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) as well as the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle) who have continued to emphasize the need to require aircraft to carry such equipment.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) indicated in the House, in answering the hon. member's question on November 6, that he is prepared to initiate such regulations. He explained to the House that the matter is not as simple as it would appear on the surface. To merely set out regulations would not solve the over-all problem at this time. What is required is a relatively low-cost locator beacon which is capable of meeting an agreed common technical standard. I should point out that a standard was established and adopted by the International Civil Aviation Organization last year. Subsequently it was incorporated in national technical specifications which were issued in May, 1970, and which are presently administered by the Department of Communications.
The specifications which I have mentioned cover four different types of emergency locator transmitter, only one of which, the personal locator beacon, could be called low-cost. I understand that there are no personal locator beacons on the market which could meet these specifications. However, one Canadian manufacturer of such equipment has recently informed the Department of Transport that he will commence production of a personal locator beacon in 1971. The availability of this equipment will be given very full consideration by the Department of Transport and by the Department of Communications, as will any other similar devices which appear on the market in future.

ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES-POWER-PROPOSED FLOODING OF SKAGIT RIVER VALLEY-SUBMISSION OF BRIEF TO STATE OF WASHINGTON INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I put a very important question to the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) on the subject of the proposed flooding of 6,000 acres of the Skagit Valley in British Columbia by the Seattle City Light Company. I should say at the outset that the fight against this agreement, which was made in January of 1967 between the province of British Columbia and Seattle City Light, has been led in Victoria by the Liberal members of the legislative assembly, notably David Brousson, and here in Ottawa by all the members of the British Columbia Liberal caucus, especially the member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle).
My concern on the issue is prompted by the firm conviction that what the Socred government has done in British Columbia is wrong and is both a disgrace and disservice to the people of our province. What they have done, Mr. Speaker, is to sell out to United States interests, for an annual rental of $5.50 per flooded acre, one of the few remaining wilderness areas in the lower mainland of our province. By agreeing to let the city of Seattle raise by 125 feet the level of the reservoir behind the Ross dam, the government of British Columbia has shown that over the protests of its own citizens it is not only willing but eager to sacrifice the last wilderness valley in the lower mainland, to flood ten miles into British Columbia, to cover over nine miles of fish spawning ground, to inundate the spring feeding ground and nursery for some 450 deer, and to do all of this just so the neon lights in Seattle can shine a little brighter at the expense of the recreational needs of our children and our children's children.
The people of British Columbia will not stand for this, Mr. Speaker. As a last resort they are looking to the federal government to provide a means of saving the Valley. In an effort to help I have introduced into this House Bill C-130, an act to amend the International River Improvements Act. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall read the effective paragraph of that bill. It is as follows:

If the government decides to accept this bill I will be very pleased indeed, and so will the scores of persons throughout British Columbia who have written asking me to do my very best to prevent this outrage. I will be just as happy if the government can stop the flooding by some alternate means. That is why this afternoon I asked the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry a question along the following lines: "In view of press reports that Mr. John Biggs, head of the Washington State Department of Ecology, has announced that his department will hold hearings on the proposed flooding of the Skagit Valley in British Columbia by Seattle City Light Company, and in view of the fact that Mr. Biggs has indicated that the government of British Columbia and the Canadian government will be encouraged to submit briefs, will the minister assure the House that the government will submit a brief in opposition to the proposed flooding?"
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the minister is prepared now to make a statement on the government's position in this regard.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of Fisheries and Forestry):
maintopic: ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES-POWER-PROPOSED FLOODING OF SKAGIT RIVER VALLEY-SUBMISSION OF BRIEF TO STATE OF WASHINGTON INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is good news that ecologists on the U.S. west coast are beginning to line up against the flooding of the Skagit Valley, particularly the flooding back mto British Columbia. My department will gladly supply any information which Canadian interveners may require when appearing at hearings held in the territory of the United States in opposition to this project. I have not yet had an opinion from the Department of External Affairs as to whether it would be proper for an agency of the
federal government to appear in a foreign court dealing with matters of this kind, but if there is no problem in this connection I would certainly want us to appear. To repeat, I qualify this, depending on advice I expect to get from the Department of External Affairs.
I should like to outline the present status of the application of Seattle Light and Power to U.S. authorities to raise the Ross dam and flood back into Canada. The Seattle city council voted in favour of its application, but action has been held up by the mayor of Seattle. The Seattle City Light and Power Company will also have to obtain permission after January 1, 1971, from the new department of ecology set up in the state of Washington and get another annual permit of the kind they have been getting every year since 1929. I understand that the new department will require a hearing to be held so there will be an opportunity, early in the new year, for interested Canadian citizens to appear in the Seattle area in opposition to this project.
Assuming the Seattle City Light and Power Company does obtain authorization from the new department of ecology, it would then be obliged to apply to the United State Federal Power Commission in Washington, D.C., which would also require a hearing to be held. A number of Canadians have been asking why we do not require hearings in Canada. Seattle City Light has been contacted on several occasions by the government of Canada with respect to the application of the International River Improvements Act, and we have yet to hear from the company in that connection.
